name: Adaliah
title: The only female ruler of Judah
summary: Athaliah, also known as Adaliah in Norwegian tradition, belonged to the Omride dynasty of the northern kingdom of Israel. Her exact family relationship is debated among scholars: the biblical texts alternately refer to her as the daughter of Ahab and as the granddaughter of Omri. Through a dynastic marriage with King Joram, she became connected to the royal house of Judah, and she introduced Baal worship into the southern kingdom. When her son Ahaziah was killed during Jehu's revolt against the Omride dynasty, Athaliah seized power and sought to wipe out the entire royal line of David to secure her position. For about six years (c. 841–835 BC), she ruled as the only woman ever to hold sole power over Israel or Judah. The secret rescue of her grandson Joash—hidden in the temple by his aunt Jehosheba, Ahaziah's sister, and the priest Jehoiada—ensured that David's dynastic line was preserved. When Jehoiada finally organized a coup, crowned Joash, and renewed the covenant between the Lord and the people, Athaliah was overthrown and executed outside the temple area. Her reign illustrates the destructiveness of foreign religious influence in Judah, but also God's faithful protection of His covenant promise to David regarding an enduring kingdom.

siblings: Ahaziah, son of Ahab, king of Israel

keyEvents.title: Marriage with Joram of Judah
keyEvents.description: Athaliah married King Joram of Judah as part of a political alliance between the Omride dynasty in Israel and the royal house of Judah, bringing Baal worship into the southern kingdom.

keyEvents.title: Negative influence on Ahaziah
keyEvents.description: After Joram's death, his son Ahaziah became king over Judah. Athaliah served as his advisor and led him to follow the ways of Ahab's house, which was evil in the Lord's sight.

keyEvents.title: Ahaziah's death at Jehu's hand
keyEvents.description: King Ahaziah of Judah was killed by Jehu during his revolt against the house of Ahab in Israel. This change of power paved the way for Athaliah's takeover in Judah.

keyEvents.title: Attempt to exterminate David's royal line
keyEvents.description: When Athaliah learned that her son was dead, she tried to wipe out the entire royal lineage of David's house to secure her own power over Judah.

keyEvents.title: Joash saved by Jehosheba and Jehoiada
keyEvents.description: The young prince Joash was secretly rescued by Jehosheba, who was Ahaziah's sister, along with the priest Jehoiada, her husband. Joash was hidden in the temple for six years while Athaliah ruled over Judah.

keyEvents.title: Athaliah's downfall and death
keyEvents.description: After six years, the priest Jehoiada organized a coup and crowned the young Joash as the rightful king. Jehoiada ordered that Athaliah be led out between the ranks and not killed in the Lord's house. She was executed at the horse gate of the king's house, and David's dynasty was restored.

versions.summary: Athaliah (also known as Ataliah) was the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel from the northern kingdom of Israel. She became queen of Judah through her marriage to King Joram, and after her son's death seized power and attempted to wipe out the entire royal line of David's house. She ruled as the only female ruler over Judah for about six years until she was overthrown by the priest Jehoiada.
versions.title: Athaliah, Queen of Judah and Mother of Ahaziah
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Jehoshabeath the Queen and Ahaziah's Mother' uses the form 'Ahaziah' while the rest of the profile consistently uses 'Ahazia'. It should be harmonized to 'Ahazia' for consistency.; [major] The role 'king' is misleading for a female ruler. Athaliah was queen/reigning queen, not king. The role should be changed to 'queen'. In addition, the role 'advisor' should be considered, as she served as an advisor to her son Ahaziah.; [minor] There is some debate among scholars whether Athaliah was the daughter or granddaughter of Omri (and thus the daughter or perhaps stepdaughter of Ahab). 2 Chron 22:2 calls her 'daughter of Omri', which can mean descendants in general. The biblical text is ambiguous, but the traditional interpretation that she was the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel is the most widespread.; [minor] Joram of Israel (also called Jehoram) was the son of Ahab and thus the brother or half-brother of Athaliah. Ahaziah of Israel was also the son of Ahab. These family relationships are reasonable, but it should be noted that the Bible does not explicitly list Athaliah's siblings – this is derived from them sharing a father (Ahab).; [minor] The death of Ahaziah is described in more detail in 2 Kgs 9:27-28. The reference to 2 Chron 22:7-9 is correct, but it could have been useful to include the 2 Kgs reference as well.; [major] The profile completely lacks footnotes. Notes should be added regarding the name form (Athaliah/Adaliah), the historical context with Baal worship, and the theological significance of David's line being preserved through Joash.

She ruled as the only female ruler over Judah for about six years (c. 841–835 BC), until she was overthrown by the priest Jehoiada, who crowned the young Joash as king. versions.title: Ruling Queen of Judah and Mother of Ahaziah
versions.reason: [minor] The text begins almost identically with version 1 ('Athaliah (also known as Athaliah) was the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel from the Northern Kingdom of Israel. She...'). Since we have been instructed to be stricter and avoid similarities with earlier versions, the opening should be rephrased.; [major] The Bible is not clear whether Athaliah was Ahab's daughter or his granddaughter (through Omri). 2 Chr 21:6 calls her 'Ahab's daughter', but 2 Kgs 8:26 calls her 'Omri's granddaughter'. Many scholars believe she may have been Omri's granddaughter rather than Ahab's biological daughter. This should be nuanced in the summary/footnotes.; [major] Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Israel are listed as siblings. If Athaliah was Ahab's daughter, this could fit, but it is uncertain. Ahaziah of Israel (son of Ahab) and Joram of Israel (son of Ahab) may be brothers, but it is unclear whether Athaliah was their sister. Furthermore, 'Ahaziah-of-Israel' is an imprecise connection – at least a footnote should comment that the family relationship is disputed.; [minor] The role 'advisor' is somewhat misleading. Athaliah was primarily a usurper – she seized power after her son's death. A more accurate role would be 'usurper' or 'ruler'. 'Regent' already covers her governing role.; [minor] The title 'Ruling Queen of Judah and Mother of Ahaziah' is clear, but could be more precise. 'Mother of Ahaziah' is only one part of her identity. A title such as 'The Only Female Ruler of Judah' would be more distinctive and descriptive.; [minor] In the footnote about dynastic marriages there is a typo: 'diplomatiisk' should be 'diplomatisk'.; [minor] The description mentions 'the horse gate at the king's palace'. According to 2 Kgs 11:16 and 2 Chr 23:15, she was killed at the horse entrance of the king's house. The wording is mostly correct but could be clarified.

versions.summary: Athaliah, also called Ahaziah in Norwegian tradition, belonged to the Omri dynasty in the northern kingdom of Israel and was most likely the daughter of King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, although her exact family relationship is debated among scholars. Through a dynastic marriage with King Joram, she became connected to the royal house of Judah, and she brought Baal worship southward. After her son Ahaziah was killed during Jehu's revolt, Athaliah seized power and attempted to wipe out the entire Davidic royal line to secure her position. For about six years (c. 841–835 BC) she ruled as the only female ruler in the history of Judah and Israel. However, through the secret rescue of her grandson Joash—hidden in the temple by Jehosheba and the priest Jehoiada—the Davidic dynastic line was preserved. When Jehoiada finally organized a coup and crowned Joash as the rightful king, Athaliah was overthrown and executed. Her story highlights both the destructiveness of foreign religious influence and God's faithful fulfillment of the covenant promise to David.
versions.title: The only female ruler of Judah
versions.reason: [major] The sibling relationship is problematic. Joram of Israel (often identified as Ahab's son) may possibly be counted as a brother, but 'akasja-av-israel' (Ahaziah of Israel) was the son of Ahab and thus potentially a brother. However, this depends on whether one accepts that Athaliah was Ahab's biological daughter. Given that the family relationship is disputed (as mentioned in the summary), it is problematic to list specific siblings as if they were certain. Moreover, it should be noted that 'Joram of Israel' (Jehoram) was also a son of Ahab, and there were several children of Ahab (for example, the 70 sons mentioned in 2 Kings 10:1). The list is simplified but acceptable as covering the most relevant siblings.; [minor] The role 'counselor' is well attested in 2 Chronicles 22:3, but the roles 'regent' or 'queen mother' (gebira) could have been a more precise addition that better reflects her formal position during Ahaziah's reign. Nevertheless, 'counselor' is not incorrect.; [minor] The summary is very well written and theologically sound. One possible improvement would be to clarify that Jehosheba was Ahaziah's sister (not merely an 'aunt' of Joash) to avoid confusion. Otherwise, the text is mature and thorough.; [minor] The footnote concerning family relationships is categorized as 'theological', but it deals primarily with historical-critical and textual analysis of various biblical texts. The categories 'linguistic' or 'historical' would have been more appropriate.; [minor] The description states that Athaliah was 'led out of the temple', but according to 2 Chronicles 23:14-15, Jehoiada ordered her to be led out between the ranks and killed outside the temple - she was executed at the horse gate of the king's house. The description is correct, but could have been slightly more precise in stating that Jehoiada explicitly commanded that she not be killed in the Lord's house.

footnotes.text: The name Athaliah (עֲתַלְיָה) is etymologically disputed. Some scholars derive it from the root עתל ('great/exalted') with the theophoric element -yah (Yahweh), meaning 'Yahweh is exalted'. Others have suggested a connection to an Akkadian root. The irony is striking: the bearer of a Yahweh-theophoric name actively worked to introduce Baal worship in Judah.

The question of Athaliah's exact lineage is disputed. 2 Chron 21:6 calls her 'daughter of Ahab', while 2 Kgs 8:26 refers to her as 'granddaughter of Omri'. Some scholars believe she was Omri's biological granddaughter and that 'daughter of Ahab' is a general designation for affiliation with the Omride dynasty. Others maintain that she was Ahab's biological daughter by Jezebel.

Athaliah is the only woman who reigned as sole ruler over either Israel or Judah. Her approximately six-year reign (c. 841–835 BC) represents a unique break in the male succession of David's dynasty and has no parallel in Israelite history.

Athaliah's attempt to exterminate the entire royal line of David has deep theological significance. God's promise to David of an eternal dynasty (2 Sam 7:12–16) was at stake. The rescue of the young Joash demonstrates God's faithfulness to His covenant with David—a covenantal line that, according to New Testament interpretation, ultimately leads to the Messiah (Matt 1:8).

The political alliance between the Omride dynasty in Israel and the royal house of Judah through dynastic marriages was part of a broader diplomatic strategy. Similar alliance marriages are well documented in the Middle East during this period, including in the Amarna letters from Egypt and Assyrian sources.

The Baal cult that Athaliah promoted in Judah had roots in Phoenician religion and was closely linked to the cult her mother Jezebel had introduced in the Northern Kingdom. Archaeological finds from Iron Age II in Judah, including cult objects and altars, testify to the spread of syncretistic religious practice in the region during this period.

In rabbinic tradition, Athaliah is seen as a parallel to her mother Jezebel—both represent the dangers of foreign religious influence on God's people. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 39b) reflects on God's protection of David's line through the miraculous rescue of the young Joash.

The priest Jehoiada's coup against Athaliah (c. 835 BC) is one of the best-documented regime changes in biblical history, with parallel accounts in both Kings and Chronicles. The detailed description of military organization, coronation rituals, and covenant renewal provides valuable insight into how power transitions occurred in ancient Judah.
